p: I approach this subject with a caution which my readers will understand. Mr Gibbon, in his fifteenth and sixteenth chapters, treated the rise of Christianity as a historian treats any other historical event, and gave such offence by the coolness of his irony that he spent years answering his clerical critics. I am a member of the Church of England and I do not share his irony on this subject. But I am also a historian, and my business here is not to preach but to set down what the record shows, which is that one of the most improbable events in the history of the world took place in the three centuries after the reign of Augustus. A small sect, founded by a Jewish teacher executed as a criminal in a minor province, became the official religion of the greatest empire on earth, and the faith, in the course of time, of a third of mankind. Whatever one believes of its divine origin, its human history is astonishing.

Of the life of Jesus, the Encyclopaedia reports that virtually all scholars of antiquity, whether believers or not, accept that he existed, that he was a Jewish preacher from Galilee, that he was baptised by John the Baptist, and that he was crucified in Jerusalem on the orders of the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, around the year thirty or thirty-three. Beyond these points, the scholars dispute much, and believers and unbelievers dispute more. Our chief sources are the four Gospels, written in Greek some forty to seventy years after his death, and the letters of the apostle Paul, which are older still.

He taught in the countryside and small towns of Galilee, in parables drawn from the lives of farmers, fishermen and housewives, of the coming of the kingdom of God. He taught love of God and of one's neighbour, including one's enemies; forgiveness without limit; the blessedness of the poor, the meek and the persecuted; and the danger of riches. He kept company with tax collectors and sinners, which scandalised the respectable, and healed the sick. He came to Jerusalem at the Passover festival, caused a disturbance in the Temple, and was arrested, handed over to the Romans, and crucified, a death the Romans reserved for slaves and rebels. His followers declared that on the third day he rose from the dead and appeared to them. Upon that proclamation the whole subsequent history rests. The historian cannot verify it; he can only observe that the disciples, who had fled in terror at his arrest, were transformed into men who would die rather than deny it.
## Paul and the spreading of the faith

At first the followers of Jesus were a sect within Judaism, worshipping in the Temple. The decisive change came through a man named Saul of Tarsus, better known by his Roman name Paul, a learned Pharisee who had persecuted the sect and was converted, he said, by a vision on the road to Damascus. Paul carried the faith to the Greek cities of Asia Minor and Greece, founding communities and writing to them letters that form a large part of the New Testament. He argued, against much opposition, that gentiles, that is non-Jews, could become Christians without first becoming Jews, without circumcision or the keeping of the Jewish law. This opened the faith to the whole Roman world. He was put to death in Rome, by tradition under the emperor Nero, about the year sixty-four or later.

Why did this faith succeed where so many others failed? Gibbon gave five reasons, with irony; let me give some without it. The Roman Empire had made travel and communication easy, and Greek a common language, so a message could pass rapidly from city to city. The faith offered a personal salvation, open equally to slave and free, man and woman, Greek and barbarian, which neither the civic gods of Rome nor the philosophies of the educated could match. Its communities cared for their poor, their widows and their sick with a devotion that impressed even their enemies; the emperor Julian, who tried to restore the old gods in the fourth century, complained that the Christians supported not only their own poor but ours as well. In times of plague, when the pagans fled, the Christians often stayed to nurse the dying, and many survived who would otherwise have died. And the faith held its members to a strict and serious morality, which, in a disordered age, was a source of strength.

The Romans were tolerant of most religions, but they required all subjects to honour the gods of the state and the divinity of the emperor, and the Christians refused. They were therefore suspected of atheism and disloyalty, and accused, by rumour, of horrible crimes. Persecution was at first local and sporadic, then, in the third century, general; the last and greatest, under the emperor Diocletian from the year three hundred and three, was terrible. It failed.

In three hundred and twelve, the general Constantine, fighting for the throne at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome, saw, so he said, a sign in the sky, and fought under the sign of Christ, and won. In the following year he and his fellow emperor granted toleration to the Christians. Constantine favoured the church throughout his reign, presided over its first general council at Nicaea, and was baptised on his deathbed. By the end of the century, under Theodosius, Christianity had become the official religion of the empire, and the old temples were closed. The persecuted had become, in some cases, persecutors, a reversal I record with sorrow, and not for the last time in this history.

Christianity brought into the Roman world ideas that were genuinely new to it: that every human soul is of infinite worth, whatever its rank; that the poor and the weak are especially beloved of God; that humility is a virtue and not a weakness; and that there is a law above the emperor. The world did not live up to these ideas, and the church often did not either. But they have worked upon the conscience of Europe for two thousand years, and have been the inspiration of its hospitals, its schools, its universities, and of the movement for the abolition of slavery, of which I shall speak in its place.
